tickets.title: `let NAME = v;` where NAME is an in-scope const silently does nothing
tickets.logos_observed: CORRECTED from the reported observation: compiles cleanly with no diagnostic, links, and runs (exit 0). However the claim that Logos 'treats it as a fresh binding that shadows the const, would print/return 5' is FALSE: instrumented with printf, `ZERO` after `let ZERO = 5;` still evaluates to 0 (the const's value), not 5. The `let ZERO = 5;` statement is silently a complete no-op at runtime: it neither introduces a new binding nor performs any refutability check nor panics on mismatch (verified with `let ZERO = 99;` followed by `printi("ZERO=%d\n", ZERO)` -> prints 'ZERO=0'). So the actual defect is worse than reported: Logos silently discards the let-statement's effect entirely while accepting it as legal, producing silently wrong values with zero diagnostic.
tickets.rust_observed: error[E0005]: refutable pattern in local binding — 'ZERO is interpreted as a constant pattern, not a new variable'; rustc requires renaming the binding.
tickets.fix_hint: sema let-pattern: a bare identifier that resolves to a const is a constant pattern (refutable, E0005); today it neither binds nor checks. See ref_shorthand_shadows_const_crash (same identifier-vs-const resolution).

tickets.title: A non-unit expression statement without `;` is accepted and acts as an early return
tickets.logos_observed: Compiles cleanly (no error). But actual runtime behavior is WORSE than the original report claimed: the program does NOT execute the following `return 0;` normally. Instead Logos treats the non-final, non-unit expression-statement's evaluated branch value as an IMPLICIT RETURN/terminator: with `if true {1} else {2}` the process exits with code 1 (the true-branch value), and with `if false {1} else {2}` it exits with code 2 (the false-branch value) -- in both cases `return 0;` never executes. A minimized single-expression case confirms this directly: `fn main() -> i32 { 5\n return 0; }` compiles with an explicit compiler warning `warning [fn main]: unreachable code after terminator` pointing at the `return 0;` line, and exits with code 5. So Logos's parser/sema misclassifies a non-final tail-position-looking expression-statement (one lacking `;`) as if it were the block's actual (terminating) tail expression, silently discarding and never executing all statements that lexically follow it in the block.
tickets.rust_observed: rustc rejects both the if/else and the minimized `5 return 0;` variants with error[E0308]: mismatched types (expected `()`, found integer), for each non-unit branch/expression.
tickets.fix_hint: sema block typing: a non-final expression statement without `;` must have type () (E0308); mlir_gen currently treats its value as the block result and skips the rest.

(1) 'primitives don't implement the operator-overload trait family at all' is FALSE: stdlib/lang/ops/ops.logos:171-236 ships impl Add for i8/i16/i32 etc (and the matching *Assign impls) -- the comment 'No primitive impls yet' at line 21 is stale relative to the impls 150 lines below it. A trailing 'return type mismatch -- expected T, got T::Output' also appears in the explicit-Rhs form but not in the working form, so it looks like a downstream symptom of the same lookup failure rather than an independent unification defect.

tickets.title: A match guard may mutate a by-value mut binding
tickets.logos_observed: Reproduced verbatim: compiles (exit 0), links, and `./f2.bin` runs returning exit 5 (classify(5) returns 5: the guard's `n=n+1=6` fails `n>100`, falls through to the catch-all `n=>n`). Extra probes (own, not in original gap) confirm the mutation is confined per-arm and does not alias the outer scrutinee: (1) with `n = n + 1000` and the guard passing, the arm body correctly returns the mutated value 1005 (exit 1005 mod 256 = 237); (2) with the guard forced false after mutating, the next arm still sees the original unmutated x=5 (exit 5), so a failed guard's mutation does not leak to later arms/alternatives; (3) with `fn classify(mut x: i32)` and computing `x + r` after the match, x is unaffected by n's mutation (exit 242 = 5+1005 mod 256), showing `mut n` is a genuine local copy, not an alias back into the caller's binding.
